doc.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Welfare, hand-me-down clothes and moving to Page Street
summary: His father had left; the family was on welfare, ate government food, then improved with the WPA era, took in roomers on Page Street and got the saxophone.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Both your parents are working, and they still could not provide for basic . . .
No. My father had gone by then. It was my mother.
Your father left home when you were how old?

Elementary school. When I went to school, we always knew who was on welfare, because they gave us clothes too. The clothes – the pants that they gave us, for the kids, they always reminded me of pallbearers pants, with the stripes and everything. It looked like everybody was going to a funeral, because we’re all wearing the same – so we knew what it was. We knew it was on welfare. We’re wearing the same clothes. Those were the lean days. Oh boy. When we got off welfare – things had gotten a little better. That was the time of the WPA and the PWA and the NRA and all those things like that. What is it? CCC camps – construction camps for the young boys. We’d go and do things. My cousin went there. I was too young. Things got better. We got off welfare. That’s when we moved to Page Street. It was a three-story house, but we didn’t need all those rooms. So my mother used to bring roomers in. $10 a week, or whatever it was like that. She was working. So the beds had to be made. I was the chambermaid. I had to make all the beds. On the weekend, I had to clean the – scrub the floors and whatnot. But we were making it, and things got a little better. I got my saxophone then. It was a summertime, and all the windows were open. It drove my neighbors crazy. “That Golson kid. There he goes again.” I was practicing in the living room, right on the front of the house. But I knew I was getting better when my mother would go to the store, and they’d put in requests. “Does he know how to play Embraceable You? Don’t Blame Me?” Then I was getting an audience. I knew I was getting better.
